question: Do Inkwell Learning's stakeholders agree on whether their account-health scores are reliable?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every statement made by Inkwell Learning participants about account-health scores or health metrics, including whether they consider the scores reliable, accurate, trustworthy or flawed, the reasons given, any doubts or caveats, and the name or role of the speaker who said it. Also extract any OrbitFlow staff statements about the health scores' accuracy or reliability.
assumptions: Question refers to the single call CALL-009 (Inkwell Learning, Prospect), so no call_types filter is applied.
'Account-health scores' is interpreted as customer health scores or similar health metrics.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: So I would not treat those scores as ground truth, and if we build a workflow that keys off them we've automated a guess.
findings.context: Darren Wu says account-health scores should not be treated as ground truth because fewer than half of CSMs update the underlying fields consistently; building a workflow on them would automate a guess. — Darren challenges Olivia's reliance on health scores; reason given is data entry inconsistency, not the scores' formula.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: I've disagreed with the framing. I think the scores are directionally useful and you think they're noise.
findings.context: Olivia Grant partly concedes Darren's point but frames the scores as directionally useful. — Olivia's response to Darren's challenge; she disagrees with the framing rather than the substance.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: I think they're noise with a trend in them, which is not the same as useful.
findings.context: Darren Wu characterises the health scores as noise with a trend in them, which he says is not the same as useful. — Darren restating his position in response to Olivia, showing continued disagreement.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: Leadership uses them, they're on the QBR deck, they're in the board pack.
findings.context: Inkwell stakeholders' disagreement on score reliability is reflected in Olivia's initial description, which Darren describes as treating the scores as reliable; the scores are on the QBR deck and in the board pack, used by leadership. — Darren's description of how leadership uses the scores, which he presents as a reason for scepticism.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: It is unreliable for anything a human has to remember to type.
findings.context: Darren and Olivia both say Snowflake usage data is the most trusted source, while the health scores are built on human-maintained fields, which Darren considers unreliable. — Darren's broader view of data trust; relevant to why he distrusts scores built on manual inputs.

findings.speaker: Maya Chen
findings.quote: Human-maintained fields are context you show to the person, not inputs the logic depends on.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff (Maya Chen) propose weighting signals by how they are produced: human-maintained fields become context shown to a person, not inputs the logic depends on. — Vendor design response to the reliability concern; a vendor statement about the design, not a claim the health scores are accurate.

findings.speaker: Darren Wu
findings.quote: The "fewer than half" is an impression, not a measurement.
findings.context: Darren says the 'fewer than half' CSM-update figure is an impression, not a measurement, and it should be measured. — Darren questions the reliability of his own estimate that underpins the scepticism about scores.

findings.speaker: Olivia Grant
findings.quote: I think the scores are directionally useful and you think they're noise.
findings.context: Inkwell's scepticism about health scores is a shared concern in the call: Darren doubts the scores; Olivia believes them directionally useful; the disagreement is not fully resolved. — Inferred from the exchange; the two stakeholders hold differing views on reliability.

draft.answer: No. Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence) distrusts the account-health scores, while Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience) sees them as directionally useful [C1][C2]. The disagreement appears unresolved, though Darren concedes his key statistic is only an impression [C3][C4]. Both agree Snowflake usage data is the most trusted source [C5].

claims.text: Darren Wu said the scores should not be treated as ground truth because fewer than half of CSMs update the underlying fields consistently, so a workflow built on them would 'automate a guess'. He later called them 'noise with a trend in them, which is not the same as useful'.
Olivia Grant partly concedes Darren's point but says the scores are directionally useful; she says she disagrees with the framing rather than the substance.
Darren noted that leadership uses the scores in the QBR deck and board pack, which he presented as a reason for scepticism.
Darren said his 'fewer than half' CSM-update figure is an impression, not a measurement, and should be measured.
Darren and Olivia both say Snowflake usage data is the most trusted source, whereas the health scores rest on human-maintained fields that Darren considers unreliable.
It appears (inferred) that the disagreement is not fully resolved in the call.

Maya Chen of OrbitFlow proposed treating human-maintained fields as context shown to a person rather than inputs the logic depends on. This is a design response, not a claim that the scores are accurate.

conflicts.description: Darren Wu says the scores are noise and not ground truth; Olivia Grant says they are directionally useful.

not_covered: Whether the scores have actually been measured for accuracy or CSM update rates
